title: 'Time travel' theory erupts over detail in 1936 New York City photo
excerpt: A 1936 photo of New York City has sparked wild time travel theories after eagle-eyed viewers spotted a man clutching a mysterious object.
content:
A 1936 photo of New York City has resurfaced, sparking wild time travel theories over a bizarre detail hidden in plain sight.

The black-and-white picture shows several people making their way through Union Square, including a man who appears to be holding an object near his ear.

The mysterious object has fueled speculation that he was using a cellphone decades before the technology became available.

Because the man has his back to the camera, the object is largely obscured, making it impossible to identify with certainty. 

One Facebook user said: ‘Looks like the guy in the middle up front is on his cell phone... hmm, time travel?’

Another posted: ‘Is that a time traveler on his phone right up front with his back to us?’

The Motorola DynaTAC 8000X, widely recognized as the first commercially available handheld cellphone, did not go on sale until 1983, 47 years after the picture was taken.

However, skeptics suggested the man wearing the vest was holding nothing more mysterious than a shortwave radio receiver, technology that had existed since the 1920s.

The black-and-white picture shows several people making their way through Union Square, including a man who appears to be holding an object near his ear. Some people online speculated it could be a cellphone, making the man a time traveler

The image was taken by Berenice Abbott, who photographed Union Square in Manhattan on July 16, 1936, as part of her iconic Changing New York documentary project for the Federal Art Project.

The photo, titled Union Square, 14th Street and Broadway, captured the bustling, energetic intersection and surrounding square during the Great Depression.

It currently resides in the Brooklyn Museum collection. 

Abbott's image has been shared numerous times on social media, where users marvel at her work and speculate that she may have captured a time traveler walking the streets of Manhattan. 

'Love the guy in the vest on his cell phone,' one Facebook user said, while another replied: 'Pretty sure that's Marty McFly.'

A similar black-and-white photo sparked the same theory after social media users claimed to have spotted a cellphone captured on a busy street in Reykjavik, Iceland in 1943 during World War II.

Kristjan Hoffman, whose family has had the photo for decades, previously shared the picture on Facebook, writing: 'The American army is taking over Icelandic splendor, as you can see.

'One thing that draws attention to this beautiful picture is that above the window, in the corner in the middle of the picture, a man is leaning and is on a cell phone.'

The post has sparked a debate, with some Facebook users agreeing with Hoffman, while others suggested the man was scratching his ear or holding a watch to his ear to make sure it was working.

Hoffman, however, pushed the time-traveler idea even further, noting: 'He’s in a stupor, standing alone and wearing a different headdress than the others and a scarf and acting like we would do today.'

The image was shared by Hoffman in 2016 but resurfaced in June, captivating the internet with the possibility of time travel. 

The photo was also shared on X, where users speculated the man could be holding a little radio.

The strange detail fueled speculation that the unidentified figure was using a cellphone decades before the technology was invented

However, the first small transistor radio was not released until the 1950s.

One user joked: 'Guy scratches ear 83 years later gets accused of being a time traveler.'

'Unless there were "secret" cell phone towers, a cell phone would be useless back then,' another X user pointed out.

Another theory was that the man may have been operating as a spy for the Axis powers.

Iceland officially remained neutral throughout World War II, but was occupied by Allied forces.

Because of its crucial strategic location, the island was taken over by the British in 1940 to prevent a German invasion, and the defense was later handed over to the US.
